extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners, patent practitioners (applicants and attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance from the MPEP on evaluating patentability issues for apparatus claims, functional and computer-implemented claim limitations, Markush claims, and the sufficiency/operability of prior art (enablement, utility, and obviousness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency and functional limitations in apparatus claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Features of an apparatus may be recited structurally or functionally. If a functional limitation is an inherent characteristic of the prior art structure, the examiner should explain that the prior art structure inherently possesses the recited limitation; the burden then shifts to applicant to establish that the prior art does not possess the characteristic relied on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat functional limitations as inherency issues when prior art structure would inherently possess the claimed function. Provide an explanation in the rejection showing the prior-art structure inherently has the characteristic. Applicant must rebut with evidence that the prior art lacks that characteristic. (Cases: In re Schreiber; Bettcher Industries v. Bunzl USA; In re Swinehart.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of operating device does not differentiate apparatus claim from prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim reciting the manner in which an apparatus is intended to be employed does not necessarily differentiate the apparatus from a prior art apparatus if the prior art teaches all structural limitations of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat recitations of intended use or manner of operation as patentably distinguishing where the prior art discloses the claimed structure. Example: Ex parte Masham — differences in amount of submersion were immaterial because structure was the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural differences control anticipation despite functional equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a prior art device performs all functions recited in the claim, it does not anticipate the claim if there is any structural difference. Means-plus-function limitations are met by structures equivalent to those in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining anticipation, compare structural elements, not merely functions. For means-plus-function language, identify corresponding structures in the specification or equivalents. (Cases: In re Donaldson; In re Robertson.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claim language breadth for computer-implemented limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional claim language not limited to a specific structure covers all devices capable of performing the recited function; if prior art discloses a device inherently capable of performing the claimed function, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102 and/or 103 may be appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim language imposes no structural limitation, give it a broad scope covering devices 'capable of' the function. Explain how the prior art device is capable of performing the recited function. (Cases: In re Translogic Technology; Intel Corp. v. U.S. ITC; In re Schreiber; In re Best; In re Ludtke; In re Swinehart.) See MPEP § 2112 for more on functional limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction for computer-implemented limitations (hardware vs software)
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer-implemented functional claim limitations may be construed to require specific structure (e.g., a combination of hardware and software) when hardware alone cannot meet the limitations; conversely, terms like 'computer' are given their broad ordinary meaning unless limited by other claim terms or the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the limitation requires enabling software or specific algorithmic structure; if hardware cannot perform the limitation absent software, construe the claim as an apparatus comprising hardware and software capable of practicing the limitation. Do not limit 'computer' to a narrow class unless the specification clearly does so. (Cases: Nazomi Communications v. Nokia; Intel Corp.; In re Paulsen.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness of automating known functions on general-purpose computers
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadly claiming an automated means to replace a manual function to accomplish the same result generally does not distinguish over the prior art; implementing a known function on a general-purpose computer may be obvious if it is the predictable use of prior art elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing obviousness of computer implementations, consider whether automation is merely the predictable application of known techniques (KSR). Applying modern electronics or Internet/browser technologies to older mechanical or information processes may be routine and therefore obvious. (Cases: KSR Int’l Co. v. Teleflex; Leapfrog Enters. v. Fisher-Price; Muniauction v. Thomson; In re Venner.) See MPEP § 2141 et seq. for further guidance and exemplary rationales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material or article worked upon does not impart patentability to apparatus claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of the material or article worked upon by a claimed structure does not, without more, impart patentability to the claims directed to the structure itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze apparatus claims based on the positively recited structural elements. A claim that merely recites the article worked on does not necessarily avoid anticipation or obviousness rejections if the structure is old. (Cases: In re Otto; In re Young; In re Casey.) Note: this line of cases is limited to machinery that works upon an article/material in its intended use.

rubrics_metrics.name: All claim limitations considered when assessing obviousness of processes (no per se product/process rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 requires a highly fact-dependent analysis considering the claimed subject matter as a whole; there are no per se rules that a conventional process becomes patentable just because it produces a nonobvious product, or vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat language reciting making or using of a nonobvious product as a material limitation of a process claim. Evaluate obviousness case-by-case; prior cases illustrate that a process yielding a novel product may be obvious and a process yielding a well-known product may be nonobvious. (Cases: In re Ochiai; In re Brouwer; TorPharm v. Ranbaxy; In re Durden; In re Albertson; In re Kanter; In re Pleuddemann; In re Kuehl; In re Mancy.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush claim principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'Markush' claim recites a list of alternatively usable members (a Markush grouping). Such claims require selection from a closed group 'consisting of' the alternative members, and are proper when the group members share a single structural similarity and a common use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat any claim that recites alternatively usable members as a Markush claim regardless of wording. Ensure the grouping is closed and that members share required structural similarity and common use. See MPEP § 2111.03 and case law (In re Harnisch; Ex parte Markush; Abbott Labs v. Baxter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush grouping format neutrality
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment of claims reciting alternatives is not governed by the particular format used; alternatives may be set forth in various phrasings but should be treated as Markush groupings when they recite alternatively usable members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not alter analysis based on phrasing (e.g., 'selected from the group consisting of' vs 'wherein the material is A, B, or C'). Markush-style claiming appears often in chemistry, pharmacology, biology, metallurgy, ceramics, and can apply to mechanical features or process steps as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush grouping indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush grouping may be indefinite if the list of alternatives is not a closed grouping or if the group is so expansive that persons skilled in the art cannot determine the metes and bounds of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate Markush claims for closure and reasonable scope. If the grouping is open-ended or too broad to permit skilled artisans to determine boundaries, raise 35 U.S.C. 112(b) issues. See MPEP § 2173.05(h) and § 2111.03 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art presumed operable/enabling when it discloses all claimed elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When a reference expressly anticipates or makes obvious all elements of a claimed invention, that reference is presumed to be operable/enabling; the burden is on applicant to rebut that presumption with evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An examiner making a proper prima facie case of anticipation need not independently investigate enablement; provide adequate notice under § 132. Applicant can submit rebuttal evidence of nonenablement. (Cases: In re Sasse; In re Antor Media Corp.) See MPEP § 716.07.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enabling-disclosure standard is independent of the type of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The level of disclosure required for an 'enabling disclosure' is the same regardless of whether the prior art is a U.S. patent, foreign patent, printed publication, or other reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not discriminate among prior art categories based on nationality or type; apply the same enablement standard across patent, foreign, and printed publications. (Case: In re Moreton.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficacy not required for prior art enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference can be enabling for anticipation even if it does not disclose a utility or proof of efficacy for the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For anticipation, it is sufficient that the claimed compound or article and a process of making it are taught by the reference; proof of efficacy is not required. (Cases: In re Schoenwald; Impax Labs v. Aventis Pharm.) See MPEP § 2122.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enabling disclosure requires sufficient detail to avoid undue experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference must disclose the subject matter in sufficient detail to enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to carry out the claimed invention; mere naming or description is insufficient if production would require undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reference merely names a compound or plant but would require undue experimentation to practice it, it is not an enabling disclosure for anticipation. Consider whether the public was in possession of the invention (In re Donohue) and whether supplementary evidence shows operability. (Cases: In re Hoeksema; Elan Pharm. v. Mayo Foundation; In re Donohue.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of secondary evidence to show operability for 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the primary reference does not itself teach how to practice the invention, secondary evidence (other patents or publications) can be cited to show public possession of the method of making or using, enabling a 35 U.S.C. 102 rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine references when the primary reference teaches every claimed element but lacks a teaching of how to make/use; secondary references can demonstrate that the public could practice the invention. (Case: In re Donohue.) See MPEP § 2131.01 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inoperative prior art may be relied upon for obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-enabling or inoperative prior art reference may nonetheless qualify as prior art for the purpose of determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not automatically discard inoperative references when assessing obviousness; analyze whether the reference would have rendered the claimed invention obvious in view of the prior art. (Cases: Beckman Instruments v. LKB Produkter AB; Symbol Techs. Inc. v. Opticon Inc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds and compositions: prior art must enable synthesis or making
rubrics_metrics.description: For chemical compounds and compositions, a prior art reference must enable one of ordinary skill in the art to make or synthesize the compound; mere naming of a compound without a known process does not constitute a description of the compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a process for making the compound was not developed until after the date of invention, the reference's mere naming is insufficient. A reference is presumed operable until applicant rebuts. Applicant must provide evidence showing that known processes could not produce the compound at the relevant time. (Cases: In re Hoeksema; In re Sasse.) See MPEP § 2121.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of unsuccessful attempts can show non-enablement for compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to prepare a compound that were unsuccessful before the date of invention can be adequate to show inoperability of a prior art reference disclosing only the structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits or experimental evidence demonstrating that known methods failed to make the claimed compound before the critical date can overcome a rejection based on a reference that merely discloses structure. However, mere assertion that an author did not attempt synthesis is insufficient if other evidence shows synthesis methods were known. (Cases: In re Wiggins; In re Donohue; In re Hoeksema.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant genetics enabling: ability to reproduce the plant is required
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims to plants, the prior art reference, combined with prior-art knowledge, must enable one of ordinary skill to reproduce (grow/cultivate) the plant; pictures alone are often insufficient unless the plant was accessible (e.g., commercially available seeds) and reproducible without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the publication plus availability (e.g., seeds, sales, or possession) put the skilled artisan in possession such that asexual reproduction is possible without undue experimentation. (Cases: In re LeGrice; Ex parte Thomson; In re Elsner.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictures/drawings may constitute enabling disclosure for apparatus/articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictures and drawings may be sufficiently enabling to put the public in possession of the article pictured, and thus may be used to reject claims to the article, provided the picture shows all claimed structural features and how they are put together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the illustration discloses all structural elements and assembly details necessary to practice the claimed article. If so, the picture can be an enabling prior art disclosure. (Case: Jockmus v. Leviton.) See MPEP § 2125 for drawings as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents are prior art for all they contain; nonpreferred embodiments can anticipate
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent reference is relevant for all it contains, not just the preferred embodiments; disclosed nonpreferred or alternative embodiments may be relied upon as prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When citing patents as prior art, consider both preferred and nonpreferred embodiments and examples; a reference need not endorse an embodiment for it to be relied upon. Disclosed alternatives may teach compositions or structures both with and without certain components. (Cases: In re Heck; Merck & Co. v. Biocraft Laboratories; Celeritas Technologies v. Rockwell.) See MPEP § 2131.05 and § 2145.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of multiple alternatives does not by itself teach away
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere disclosure of more than one alternative in a reference does not constitute a teaching away from any of those alternatives because such disclosure does not criticize, discredit, or otherwise discourage the claimed solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat a reference as teaching away solely because it presents multiple options; look for explicit criticism or discouragement of the claimed alternative. (Case: re Fulton.)
